blocks.p: Then, when a suitable time had been set, they brought them out for trial, in order to condemn them. When the time came, they were brought before their enemies and charged. The judge’s name was Lord Hate-good. Their indictment was the same in substance, though it varied somewhat in form, and it read as follows:

“That they were enemies to and disturbers of the town’s trade; that they had caused commotion and division in the town, and had won a party over to their own most dangerous opinions, in contempt of the law of their prince.”

v: Now, Faithful, play the man; speak for
Fear not the malice of the wicked, nor
Speak boldly, man; the truth is on your side.
Die for it, and to life in triumph ride.

blocks.p: Then Faithful began his answer. He said that he had only set himself against what had set itself against Him who is higher than the highest.

“And as for disturbance,” he said, “I make none, being a man of peace myself. Those who were won over to us were won by seeing our truth and innocence, and they have only turned from the worse to the better. And as for the king you speak of, since he is Beelzebub, the enemy of our Lord, I defy him and all his angels.”

Then it was proclaimed that anyone who had anything to say for their lord the king against the prisoner at the bar should come forward at once and give evidence. So three witnesses came in: Envy, Superstition, and Mr. Toady. They were asked whether they knew the prisoner at the bar, and what they had to say against him on behalf of their lord the king.
Then Envy stood up and said, in effect, “My Lord, I have known this man a long time, and I will testify on my oath before this honorable bench that he is—”
“Wait!” said the judge. “Swear him in.”
So they swore him in, and he went on.

“My Lord, this man, in spite of his respectable name, is one of the vilest men in our country. He has no regard for prince or people, law or custom, but does all he can to fill everyone’s head with certain disloyal notions of his, which in general he calls ‘principles of faith and holiness.’ And in particular, I once heard him say myself that Christianity and the customs of our town of Vanity were diametrically opposed, and could never be reconciled. By saying so, my Lord, he condemns at one stroke not only all our praiseworthy practices, but us for practicing them.”
“Have you anything more to say?” said the judge.

“My Lord, I could say much more, only I would not weary the court. But if need be, when the other gentlemen have given their evidence, I will add to my testimony against him, rather than let anything be lacking that would finish him off.”

So he was told to stand aside. Then they called Superstition, and told him to look at the prisoner, and asked what he could say against him on behalf of their lord the king. They swore him in, and he began.

“My Lord, I have no great acquaintance with this man, nor do I want to know him any better. But this much I do know, that he is a thoroughly dangerous fellow, from a conversation I had with him in this town the other day. As I talked with him, I heard him say that our religion was worthless, and such that no one could possibly please God by it. Your Lordship knows very well what must follow from such a statement: namely, that our worship is still in vain, that we are still in our sins, and that in the end we shall be damned. And that is what I have to say.”
Then Mr. Toady was sworn in and told to say what he knew against the prisoner at the bar on behalf of their lord the king.

“My Lord, and all you gentlemen: I have known this fellow a long time, and I have heard him say things that should never have been said. He has slandered our noble prince Beelzebub, and spoken with contempt of his honorable friends, whose names are Lord Old Man, Lord Carnal Delight, Lord Luxurious, Lord Desire of Vain Glory, my old Lord Lechery, and Sir Having Greedy, along with all the rest of our nobility. Moreover, he has said that if everyone thought as he does, not one of these noblemen would be allowed to remain in this town, if he could help it. Besides that, he has not been afraid to slander you, my Lord, who are now appointed to be his judge, calling you an ungodly villain, along with many other such vile names, with which he has bespattered most of the gentry of our town.”
When Mr. Toady had told his tale, the judge turned to the prisoner at the bar and said, “You renegade, heretic, and traitor, have you heard what these honest gentlemen have testified against you?”
“May I speak a few words in my own defense?” said Faithful.

“You wretch! You wretch! You deserve to live no longer, but to be put to death on the spot. Yet so that everyone may see how gentle we are toward you, let us hear what you have to say, you vile renegade.”

“I say, then,” said Faithful, “first, in answer to what Mr. Envy has said: I never said anything but this, that whatever rules, or laws, or customs, or people are flatly against the Word of God are diametrically opposed to Christianity. If I have said anything wrong in this, convince me of my error, and I am ready to retract it here before you.

“Second, as to Mr. Superstition and his charge against me: I said only this, that the worship of God requires a faith that comes from God; but there can be no such faith without God’s own revelation of his will. Therefore, whatever is pushed into the worship of God that does not agree with what God has revealed can only be done by a merely human faith, and that faith will not lead to eternal life.

“Third, as to what Mr. Toady has said, I say (leaving aside his claim that I slander people, and the like) that the prince of this town, with all the rabble who attend him, whom this gentleman has named, are more fit to live in hell than in this town and country. And so, the Lord have mercy on me!”
Then the judge called to the jury, who all this time had stood by to listen and observe.

“Gentlemen of the jury, you see this man about whom there has been such an uproar in this town. You have heard what these worthy gentlemen have testified against him. You have also heard his reply and confession. It now lies with you to hang him or to save his life. But first I think it right to instruct you in our law.

“There was an act passed in the days of Pharaoh the Great, a servant of our prince, that so that those of a contrary religion would not multiply and grow too strong for him, their male children should be thrown into the river. [Exo. 1:22] There was also an act passed in the days of Nebuchadnezzar the Great, another of his servants, that whoever would not fall down and worship his golden image should be thrown into a fiery furnace. [Dan. 3:6] There was also an act passed in the days of Darius, that whoever, for a certain period, called on any god but him should be thrown into the lions’ den. [Dan. 6] Now this rebel has broken the substance of these laws, not only in thought, which is not to be tolerated, but also in word and deed, which is therefore absolutely intolerable.

“As for Pharaoh’s law, it was made on a supposition, to prevent mischief before any crime had been committed; but here a crime is plain to see. As for the second and third, you see that he argues against our religion. And for the treason he has confessed, he deserves to die.”

Then the jury went out. Their names were Mr. Blind-man, Mr. No-good, Mr. Malice, Mr. Love-lust, Mr. Live-loose, Mr. Hothead, Mr. Haughty, Mr. Enmity, Mr. Liar, Mr. Cruelty, Mr. Hate-light, and Mr. Implacable. Each of them gave his private verdict against him among themselves, and afterward they agreed unanimously to bring him in guilty before the judge.
First, among themselves, Mr. Blind-man, the foreman, said, “I see clearly that this man is a heretic.”
Then Mr. No-good said, “Away with such a fellow from the earth.”
“Yes,” said Mr. Malice, “for I hate the very look of him.”
Then Mr. Love-lust said, “I could never stand him.”
“Nor I,” said Mr. Live-loose, “for he was always condemning my way of life.”
“Hang him, hang him,” said Mr. Hothead.
“A miserable wretch,” said Mr. Haughty.
“My heart rises against him,” said Mr. Enmity.
“He is a rogue,” said Mr. Liar.
“Hanging is too good for him,” said Mr. Cruelty.
“Let’s get him out of the way,” said Mr. Hate-light.
Then Mr. Implacable said, “If I were given the whole world, I could not be reconciled to him. So let us bring him in guilty of death at once.”
And so they did. He was immediately condemned to be taken from where he was to the place he had come from, and there to be put to the cruelest death that could be devised.

So they brought him out to do with him according to their law. First they whipped him, then they beat him with their fists, then they slashed his flesh with knives; after that they stoned him with stones, then pierced him with their swords; and last of all they burned him to ashes at the stake. So Faithful came to his end.

Now I saw that behind the crowd there stood a chariot and a pair of horses, waiting for Faithful. As soon as his enemies had finished with him, he was taken up into it and carried straight up through the clouds, with the sound of a trumpet, by the nearest way to the Celestial Gate.

v: Brave Faithful, bravely done in word and deed!
Judge, witnesses, and jury have, instead
of overcoming you, but shown their rage:
when they are dead, you’ll live from age to age.

blocks.p: (That is, in the new heaven and new earth.)
